title: Review: Translation; Genes, the genetic code and genomes; Amino acids and peptide bonds
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: GE03#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM07#t3 term and clue written for the game; BM07#t2 term and clue written for the game; GE05a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM07#N.4a, GE03#N.3a, GE05a#N.7, BM07#N.13, GE03#N.5a, GE05a#N.4, BM07#N.6a, GE05a#N.10, BM07#N.2a. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Degenerate code
items.clue: Feature meaning that most amino acids are specified by more than one triplet.

items.label: R group
items.clue: The side chain: the only part that differs between the twenty protein monomers

items.label: Peptide bond
items.clue: Covalent –CO–NH– link made when a carboxyl and an amine lose one water molecule

items.label: Translation
items.clue: Using the base sequence of mRNA to build the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide.

questions.stem: Two amino acids react to form a dipeptide. Which statement describes this reaction?

options.text: The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amine group of the other, and water is released.
A molecule of water is taken in to provide the atoms needed to link the two amino acids together.
The R-group of one amino acid bonds to the R-group of the other, forming the peptide bond between them.
The amine group of one amino acid forms a hydrogen bond with the carboxyl group of the other, and no water is released.

questions.explanation: Condensation: amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water. The peptide bond forms between the carbon of the carboxyl group and the nitrogen of the amine group.

questions.stem: Why does the genetic code use codons of three bases rather than two?

options.text: Two bases would give 16 codons, which is close enough to 20 for nearly all the amino acids to be coded.
Three bases allow each codon to code for up to three different amino acids whenever these are needed.
Three bases let the ribosome start reading at any point, since any group of three is a codon.
Three bases give 64 possible codons, enough for 20 amino acids, whereas two bases give only 16.

questions.explanation: 4 × 4 = 16 is fewer than 20; 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 is more than enough, so a triplet code is the shortest that works.

questions.stem: An antibiotic stops the ribosome from moving along the mRNA but does not affect the binding of tRNAs or the formation of peptide bonds. What effect will this have on translation of an mRNA?

options.text: Only the first peptide bond forms, since the next codon cannot be moved into place for a tRNA to bind.
Translation is unaffected, because all the tRNAs bind along the mRNA before any peptide bonds are formed.
Translation is unaffected, because each tRNA leaves the ribosome before the next one binds to the mRNA.
The chain still grows, because each tRNA stays attached to its amino acid and the next tRNA simply joins onto it.

questions.stem: Two short polypeptides, P and Q, are each made of the same five amino acids, but the amino acids are joined in a different order in P and in Q. Which statement about P and Q is correct?

options.text: They are the same molecule, because they contain exactly the same amino acids.
They have the same properties, because a polypeptide's properties come from its amine and carboxyl groups.
They are different polypeptides, because their R groups sit in different positions along the chain.
They are different polypeptides, because their peptide bonds join different pairs of R groups.

questions.explanation: Each chain has four peptide bonds and the same backbone, but the R groups are in a different order. Order is one of the three sources of variety, with chain length and repeats.

questions.stem: The genetic code is described as degenerate. What does this mean?

options.text: Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.
A single codon can code for two or more different amino acids.
The same codons code for the same amino acids in all organisms.
Some amino acids are coded for by two bases and some by three bases.

questions.explanation: 61 codons code for 20 amino acids; for example GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for glycine.

questions.stem: A cell contains many different kinds of tRNA molecule. What is the role of a tRNA during translation?

options.text: It binds to a codon first and then collects from the cytoplasm whichever amino acid that codon specifies.
It brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome and pairs its anticodon with the matching codon on the mRNA.
It delivers an amino acid and remains bonded to it, becoming part of the finished polypeptide chain.
It carries the mRNA bases that the ribosome converts into the amino acids of the polypeptide.

questions.explanation: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to the codons for that amino acid, so base pairing at the ribosome delivers the amino acid the codon specifies.

questions.stem: A polypeptide of 150 amino acids is assembled by condensation reactions. How does the number of water molecules change as the whole chain is formed?

options.text: 150 released
298 released
149 released
149 consumed

questions.explanation: Each condensation forms one peptide bond and releases one water molecule. A chain of 150 needs 149 bonds: 149 water molecules.

questions.stem: The coding region of an mRNA, from the first nucleotide of the start codon to the last nucleotide of the stop codon, is 903 nucleotides long. How many amino acids does the polypeptide translated from this region contain?
questions.explanation: 903 ÷ 3 = 301 codons. AUG codes for methionine and the stop codon codes for nothing, so the polypeptide has 301 − 1 = 300 amino acids.

questions.stem: Which feature is shared by all 20 of the amino acids that are coded for in the genetic code?

options.text: The R-group is identical in every amino acid, and the amine and carboxyl groups are what vary.
An amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and an R-group are all bonded to one alpha carbon atom.
The amine group is bonded directly to the carbon atom of the carboxyl group, with no carbon between.
The amine group is an NH₃ group, with the same structure as a molecule of ammonia.

questions.explanation: This is the general structure: a central (alpha) carbon carrying the amine group, the carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and the R-group. Only the R-group differs between the 20.
